mainTopic: Eating after the מצה; whether מצה and מרור are Torah or rabbinic obligations today; falling asleep during the פסח meal.
overview: This עמוד first finishes a debate over two versions of שמואל's ruling about eating after-meal foods (אפיקומן) after the מצה. Each time, the גמרא answers a proof or a challenge by showing that a source only mentions the more surprising case ('לא מיבעיא'). Then רבא rules that eating מצה today is a Torah obligation, but מרור is only rabbinic, because the Torah ties מרור to the קרבן פסח while it commands מצה again in a separate verse, 'בערב תאכלו מצות'. רב אחא בר יעקב disagrees and holds that both are rabbinic today. He uses that verse to teach that a טמא or someone on a דרך רחוקה must still eat מצה and מרור. רבא answers that this is already known from the ערל and the בן נכר, and רב אחא בר יעקב replies that both cases need their own verse. A ברייתא then supports רבא: eating מצה is optional during the week of פסח, but on the first night it is a fixed obligation, even without a בית המקדש. Finally, a new משנה begins about people who fall asleep in the middle of eating the קרבן פסח.

steps.title: The proof ends: eating מצה first is not good
steps.stepSummary: This is the final words of a proof that began on the previous עמוד: the ברייתא implies that eating מצה first, before other foods, is not acceptable.
steps.simpleTranslation: But first (before the other foods) — no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a proof it started on the previous עמוד. The ברייתא says to eat מצה 'last', so eating it first seems to be not allowed, which supports רב יהודה's version of שמואל: no after-meal foods once you eat מצה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lets a person fill up on cakes as long as he eats a כזית of מצה at the end. The inference is: מצה must come last and nothing should follow it. That fits the rule אין מפטירין אחר המצה אפיקומן.

keyTerms.meaning: first, at the beginning
no, not

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not a new statement. It is the tail of a דיוק (inference) from a ברייתא that the גמרא quoted at the end of the previous עמוד.

phrases.english: But first — no.
phrases.notes: Putting it together: at the end, yes; at the start, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the proof that began on the previous עמוד.
steps.raayaObject: רב יהודה's version of שמואל: no אפיקומן after מצה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about סופגנין: 'provided he eats a כזית of מצה last', which implies מצה should not come first.

steps.title: Rejecting the proof: the ברייתא is teaching the bigger חידוש
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. The ברייתא says 'last' only because that is the surprising case. Eating מצה first is obviously fine.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is speaking in a 'needless to say' style. Needless to say, eating מצה first is fine, since he eats it with an appetite. But eating it last, you might think he would end up eating it as overstuffed eating and would not fulfill the מצוה. So the ברייתא teaches us that even last is fine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof. The ברייתא never meant that eating מצה first is bad; it chose the harder case to teach something new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating מצה first is obviously good, because you are hungry and eat it properly. Eating it after you are stuffed might seem to be אכילה גסה, which does not count as proper eating. The ברייתא teaches that even this works, so it says nothing about whether other foods may follow מצה.

keyTerms.meaning: needless to say; it is obvious (a style that mentions the harder case)
with appetite, while hungry
overstuffed eating, which does not count as proper eating
I might have said (you would have thought)
it teaches us (something new)

steps.whyThisMatters: The 'לא מיבעיא' move is a key tool. A text that mentions only one case may be choosing the surprising case, not excluding the other one. The same move comes back in step 5.

phrases.english: It is speaking in a 'needless to say' style.
Needless to say, first (eating matza before) —
since he eats it with an appetite (it is fine);
but last (after the cakes),
perhaps he will come to eat it as overstuffed eating —
phrases.notes: He is already full from the cakes.

phrases.english: I might say he does not fulfill it,
so it teaches us that he does.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from step 1.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof. רב יהודה's ruling itself still stands.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The inference 'first, no' is wrong. The ברייתא mentions 'last' as the bigger חידוש (the אכילה גסה concern), not to rule out 'first'.

steps.title: מר זוטרא's version: one may eat אפיקומן after מצה
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא reports שמואל's ruling the opposite way: one MAY eat after-meal foods after the מצה.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא taught it this way: רב יוסף said in the name of רב יהודה in the name of שמואל: one may conclude with אפיקומן after the מצה.
steps.whatsHappening: A second tradition of the same ruling is brought, and it says the opposite. In this version, eating dessert after מצה is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, שמואל said אין מפטירין, meaning no after-meal food after מצה. Here מר זוטרא's chain of tradition records מפטירין, meaning you may. The rest of this passage tests this lenient version.

keyTerms.meaning: taught (the tradition) this way
conclude (the meal) with; may finish with
here: dessert or after-meal foods (not the hidden מצה of today)

steps.confusionAlert: In this סוגיא, אפיקומן means after-meal treats or extra foods. It does NOT mean the piece of מצה we hide and eat at the end of the סדר.

phrases.english: Mar Zutra taught it this way:
phrases.notes: Here comes a different version of the teaching.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה
phrases.english: Rav Yosef said that Rav Yehuda said
that Shmuel said:
One may conclude after the matza with afikoman (dessert).
phrases.notes: The opposite of the first version.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a competing version of the ruling discussed in steps 1 and 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may eat after-meal foods (אפיקומן) after the מצה.

steps.title: Trying to support מר זוטרא's version from the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The משנה forbids אפיקומן after the קרבן פסח. That seems to imply it is allowed after מצה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say the משנה supports him: 'One may not conclude after the פסח with אפיקומן'? After the פסח it is not allowed, but after מצה, one may conclude.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to prove the lenient version from our משנה, which mentions only the קרבן פסח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's ban is limited to after the פסח. The דיוק (inference) is that after מצה there is no ban, which matches מר זוטרא's version of שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: shall we say it supports him?
the Paschal lamb (קרבן פסח)

phrases.english: Shall we say (the Mishnah) supports him:
'One may not conclude after the Paschal lamb with afikoman.'
After the Paschal lamb it is not allowed,
but after matza — one may conclude.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Seeks a source for the ruling in step 3.
steps.raayaObject: מר זוטרא's version: אפיקומן is allowed after מצה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה: אין מפטירין אחר הפסח אפיקומן, which mentions only the פסח.

steps.title: Rejecting the proof: the משנה teaches the harder case
steps.stepSummary: The משנה mentions the פסח only because it is the surprising case. After מצה, it is obviously forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is speaking in a 'needless to say' style. Needless to say, after מצה it is forbidden, since its taste is not strong. But after the פסח, you might think it is allowed, so the משנה teaches us that it is forbidden even then.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof using the same 'לא מיבעיא' move as in step 2.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מצה has a weak taste, so dessert would easily wipe it out, and it should obviously not follow מצה. The פסח meat has a strong taste that would stay, so one might think dessert after it is fine. The משנה teaches the חידוש that even after the פסח it is forbidden, so it proves nothing about permitting it after מצה.

keyTerms.meaning: is much, strong
its taste

phrases.english: It is speaking in a 'needless to say' style.
Needless to say, after matza (it is forbidden) —
since its taste is not strong;
phrases.notes: Eating dessert afterward would wipe out its taste.

phrases.english: but after the Paschal lamb —
I might say it is not forbidden,
so it teaches us that it is.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from step 4.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof is removed. מר זוטרא's version is not yet refuted.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The משנה names the פסח as the bigger חידוש, not to exclude מצה.

steps.title: Challenge to מר זוטרא's version from the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא requires the מצה to be eaten last, which implies nothing should come after it. That contradicts the lenient version.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: With sponge cakes, honey-fried cakes, and honey cakes, a person may fill his stomach, as long as he eats a כזית of מצה last. Last, yes; first, no!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks מר זוטרא's lenient version using the same ברייתא from before. If מצה must come last, eating dessert after מצה seems wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says 'last, yes; first, no.' That means foods should not follow the מצה, which is the opposite of מפטירין אחר המצה. The answer to this challenge comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: they raised an objection (from a ברייתא)
sponge cakes (unleavened)
his stomach
an olive-sized amount (minimum for the מצוה)
yes

steps.confusionAlert: This is the same ברייתא that was a proof (steps 1–2) for the first version. Now it is a challenge to מר זוטרא's version. One source can play different roles depending on which version is being tested.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
Sponge cakes, honey-fried cakes, and honey cakes —
a person may fill his stomach with them,
provided that he eats an olive-bulk of matza last.
Last — yes;
first — no!
phrases.notes: So nothing should follow the matza.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the support attempt failed, the גמרא now challenges the lenient version directly.
steps.kashyaTarget: מר זוטרא's version: מפטירין אחר המצה אפיקומן.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא demands that מצה be last ('first, no'), which implies foods may not follow מצה.

steps.title: The ברייתא Teaches That Even Eating מצה Last Works
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is in 'needless to say' style. Eating מצה first is obviously fine. It mentions eating it last to teach that even when you are full, you still fulfill the מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is saying 'needless to say.' Needless to say that eating מצה first works, since you eat it with appetite. But eating it last, when you might eat it while stuffed, you might think it does not count. So it teaches us that it does count.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 6. The ברייתא does not demand that מצה be eaten last. It only teaches that eating it last is still valid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge read 'last' as a requirement, which would mean nothing may be eaten after the מצה. The answer reads 'last' as the surprising case: when you are full, it looks like אכילה גסה, which might not count as real eating. The ברייתא tells us it still counts, so it no longer contradicts the lenient version.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is saying needless to say': it mentions the surprising case, and the obvious case is assumed.
With appetite, while still hungry.
Eating while overly full (stuffed). Such eating may not count as proper 'eating.'
'It teaches us': the new point being taught.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read 'last' in the ברייתא as a requirement. It is a permission: even if you eat the מצה last, it still counts.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא's 'last' is the surprising case (eating while full), not a rule that the מצה must be last. So the challenge is answered.

phrases.english: It is saying 'needless to say.'
Needless to say, if one eats it first —
since he eats it with appetite,
but if he eats it last,
when he comes to eat it as overstuffed eating —
I might say he does not fulfill his obligation,
so it teaches us that he does.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the source: the 'last' case is a 'needless to say' case, not a requirement.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא requires מצה to be eaten last, so nothing may follow it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא only teaches that even eating מצה last, while full, still fulfills the מצוה.

steps.title: רבא: מצה Today Is Torah Law, מרור Is Rabbinic
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that even after the בית המקדש was destroyed, eating מצה is a Torah obligation. Eating מרור today is only rabbinic.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: מצה nowadays is a Torah obligation, and מרור is a rabbinic one.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רבא gives a ruling that separates מצה from מרור in our times.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Today there is no קרבן פסח. רבא says the Torah מצוה of מצה still applies anyway, but the Torah מצוה of מרור does not. Today's מרור is a rabbinic enactment that keeps the practice alive.

keyTerms.meaning: Nowadays, when there is no בית המקדש.
A Torah-level obligation.
A rabbinic-level obligation.
Bitter herbs.

steps.whyThisMatters: This ruling decides whether eating מצה and מרור at the סדר today is a Torah obligation or only a rabbinic one.

phrases.english: Rava said:
Matza nowadays is by Torah law,
and bitter herbs are by rabbinic law.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: מַצָּה בִּזְמַן הַזֶּה דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic after the previous discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Today, מצה is a Torah obligation and מרור is a rabbinic one.

steps.title: Why Is מרור Different?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why מרור should be treated differently from מצה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is different about מרור?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רבא's split. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both foods are part of the same סדר, so treating them differently needs a source. The question asks what that source is.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What is different?' A request for the reason two things are treated differently.

phrases.english: And what is different about bitter herbs?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of רבא's ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason מרור is only rabbinic today while מצה remains a Torah obligation.

steps.title: מרור Depends on the קרבן פסח
steps.stepSummary: The verse 'על מצות ומרורים' links מרור to the קרבן פסח. When there is a פסח, there is a Torah מצוה of מרור. When there is no פסח, there is none.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written, 'With מצות and bitter herbs [they shall eat it].' When there is a פסח, there is מרור. When there is no פסח, there is no מרור.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The verse makes מרור part of eating the קרבן פסח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse says to eat the פסח 'with' מרור, so מרור is attached to the קרבן. With no קרבן today, the Torah obligation of מרור falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: 'With מצות and bitter herbs' (במדבר ט:יא), said about eating the קרבן פסח.
The קרבן פסח, the Paschal lamb.

phrases.english: As it is written: 'With matzot and bitter herbs,'
when there is a Paschal lamb, there are bitter herbs,
and when there is no Paschal lamb, there are no bitter herbs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The Torah obligation of מרור is attached to the קרבן פסח, so it does not apply without one.

steps.title: But מצה Is in the Same Verse
steps.stepSummary: מצה appears in the very same verse with מרור. So מצה should also depend on the פסח and be only rabbinic today.
steps.simpleTranslation: מצה too: isn't it written, 'With מצות and bitter herbs'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reasoning just given. The same verse mentions מצה, so the same logic should apply to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If being attached to the פסח in this verse cancels מרור today, it should cancel מצה too. That would undo רבא's split between the two.

keyTerms.meaning: 'But isn't it written?' Bringing a verse as a challenge.

phrases.english: Matza too,
isn't it written: 'With matzot and bitter herbs'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the derivation in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's distinction between מצה and מרור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The verse links both foods equally to the פסח, so both should lapse without it.

steps.title: מצה Has Its Own Separate Verse
steps.stepSummary: The Torah repeats the מצוה of מצה in a separate verse, 'בערב תאכלו מצות.' That makes מצה an independent obligation that does not depend on the פסח.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse went back and repeated מצה: 'In the evening you shall eat מצות.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge in defense of רבא. מצה gets a second, independent verse, and מרור does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the Torah commands מצה again by itself (שמות יב:יח), it is not only an add-on to the פסח. So the Torah obligation of מצה stays even without a קרבן.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The verse went back to it again': the Torah repeated the מצוה separately.
'In the evening you shall eat מצות' (שמות יב:יח).

phrases.english: With matza, the verse repeated it again:
'In the evening you shall eat matzot.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: An additional verse creates an independent obligation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: מצה depends on the פסח just like מרור.
steps.terutzMaskana: מצה has its own verse, so it is a Torah obligation even today.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבא, מרור depends on the פסח, but מצה stands on its own because of 'בערב תאכלו מצות.'

steps.title: רב אחא בר יעקב: Both Are Rabbinic Today
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר יעקב disagrees with רבא. Today both מצה and מרור are only rabbinic.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב אחא בר יעקב said: both this and that are rabbinic.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second opinion that argues with רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אחא בר יעקב holds that both foods depend on the קרבן פסח. So without the קרבן, neither one is a Torah obligation today.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Both this and that': here, both מצה and מרור.
An אמורא who disagrees with רבא here.

phrases.english: And Rav Acha bar Yaakov said:
Both this and that are by rabbinic law.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבא's ruling in step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Today, both מצה and מרור are rabbinic obligations.

steps.title: But What About the Separate מצה Verse?
steps.stepSummary: The verse 'בערב תאכלו מצות' seems to make מצה an independent Torah obligation. So how can רב אחא בר יעקב say it is rabbinic?
steps.simpleTranslation: But isn't it written, 'In the evening you shall eat מצות'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב אחא בר יעקב using the same verse that supported רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: That verse is exactly what made מצה independent of the פסח for רבא. If רב אחא בר יעקב ignores it, he needs to explain what the verse is for.

keyTerms.meaning: 'But isn't it written?' A strong challenge from a verse.

phrases.english: But isn't it written:
'In the evening you shall eat matzot'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב אחא בר יעקב's view in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אחא בר יעקב's claim that מצה today is rabbinic.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A separate verse for מצה should make it independent of the פסח, and therefore a Torah obligation today.

steps.title: The Verse Teaches About the Impure and the Distant Traveler
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר יעקב uses the verse for a different lesson. A person who is טמא or on a דרך רחוקה cannot bring the פסח, but must still eat מצה and מרור.
steps.simpleTranslation: He needs that verse for a person who is impure or was on a distant road. You might have thought that since they do not eat the פסח, they also do not eat מצה and מרור. So it teaches us that they do.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for רב אחא בר יעקב. The extra verse teaches a different law, so it does not prove that מצה is a Torah obligation today.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In בית המקדש times, a טמא person or one far away skips the first פסח. One might think they also skip מצה and מרור. The verse teaches that they must still eat them. So the verse is about people who cannot bring the פסח while the קרבן exists, not about times when there is no קרבן at all.

keyTerms.meaning: 'He needs it' for a different teaching.
A ritually impure person, who cannot bring the קרבן פסח.
A distant road: someone too far from ירושלים to bring the פסח on time.
'It would enter your mind to say': the mistaken first assumption.

steps.confusionAlert: The verse here does not discuss our times. It discusses a person who misses the פסח while the בית המקדש is standing. That is why רב אחא בר יעקב can still say מצה today is rabbinic.
steps.whatToRemember: רבא: מצה today is a Torah obligation, because it has its own verse. רב אחא בר יעקב: both מצה and מרור are rabbinic today, and the extra verse teaches that the טמא and the far-away traveler must still eat מצה and מרור.
steps.whyThisMatters: This disagreement decides whether eating מצה at the סדר today is a Torah obligation or a rabbinic one.

phrases.english: He needs that verse
for one who is impure or who was on a distant road,
for it would enter your mind to say:
since they do not eat the Paschal lamb —
they should not eat matza and bitter herbs either,
so it teaches us that they must.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהִיא מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְטָמֵא וְשֶׁהָיָה בְּדֶרֶךְ רְחוֹקָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 14 on behalf of רב אחא בר יעקב.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redirecting the verse to a different teaching.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Someone who cannot eat the פסח is also exempt from מצה and מרור.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even the טמא and the far-away traveler must eat מצה and מרור. The verse does not make מצה a Torah obligation when there is no קרבן at all.

steps.title: רבא explains why he does not need the verse for a טמא
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that a טמא and one on a דרך רחוקה obviously must eat מצה, because they are no worse than an ערל or a בן נכר.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא would answer you: A טמא and someone on a far-away road do not need a verse to teach that they eat מצה. They are no worse than an ערל or a בן נכר, who also eat מצה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows how רבא would answer רב אחא בר יעקב's reading of the verse 'בערב תאכלו מצות'. רבא says the lesson about a טמא is obvious, so the verse is still available to make מצה its own Torah obligation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אחא בר יעקב used the verse to teach that a טמא or one on a דרך רחוקה still eats מצה. רבא says no verse is needed for that. We already know that an ערל and a בן נכר cannot eat the פסח but still eat מצה, and a טמא is no worse than them. So the verse is free to teach רבא's point: מצה is an independent חיוב even today.

keyTerms.meaning: No verse is needed (the law is already known)
They are no worse / no weaker
An uncircumcised man, who may not eat the קרבן פסח
A Jew who has turned away from the מצוות. He may not eat the פסח but is still obligated in מצה.

phrases.english: And Rava would say to you:
An impure person and one who was on a distant road
do not need a verse,
phrases.notes: No verse is needed to teach that they must eat מצה.

phrases.english: because they are no worse than an uncircumcised man or an alien.
phrases.notes: An ערל and a בן נכר also cannot eat the פסח, yet they still eat מצה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends רבא against the reading of the verse that רב אחא בר יעקב gave in Step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Removing the need for the other side's reading: the lesson is already known through a קל וחומר-style comparison, so the verse stays free for רבא's lesson.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The verse 'בערב תאכלו מצות' is needed to teach that a טמא eats מצה, so it cannot prove that מצה is an independent Torah obligation.
steps.terutzMaskana: A טמא is no worse than an ערל or a בן נכר, so no verse is needed for him. The verse teaches that מצה is an independent חיוב.

steps.title: A ברייתא proves that an ערל eats מצה and מרור
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reads 'בו' in the verse 'כל ערל לא יאכל בו' to mean that an ערל may not eat the פסח, but he does eat מצה and מרור.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: 'No ערל may eat of it.' He may not eat 'of it,' meaning the פסח. But he does eat מצה and מרור.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source for רבא's claim that an ערל still eats מצה. The word 'בו' ('of it') limits the ban to the פסח alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse could have just said 'an ערל may not eat.' The word 'בו' narrows the ban to the קרבן פסח. So the ערל is still obligated in מצה and מרור. This is the base case that רבא compares the טמא to.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא
Shall not eat of it (of the פסח)
However / but

phrases.english: As it was taught: 'No uncircumcised man shall eat of it' —
'of it' he does not eat,
phrases.notes: Only the פסח itself is off-limits to him.

phrases.english: but he does eat matza and bitter herbs.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: כׇּל עָרֵל לֹא יֹאכַל בּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the comparison to an ערל made in Step 16.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's claim that someone who cannot eat the פסח still eats מצה and מרור.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא reading 'בו' in 'כל ערל לא יאכל בו' (שמות יב:מח) as limiting the ban to the פסח.

steps.title: How does רב אחא בר יעקב respond?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רב אחא בר יעקב deals with רבא's argument that no verse is needed for a טמא.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one (רב אחא בר יעקב)? How does he answer this?
steps.whatsHappening: This is a short setup question. The גמרא is about to explain why רב אחא בר יעקב still needs a verse for the טמא, even though the ערל already teaches the same law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא said the ערל case already covers the טמא, so the verse is not needed. That seems to weaken רב אחא בר יעקב's reading. The גמרא now asks for his response.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one (how does he answer?)

phrases.english: And the other?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns רבא's point back onto רב אחא בר יעקב and asks for his answer.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רב אחא בר יעקב needs the verse for a טמא if the ערל case already teaches it.

steps.title: Both cases need their own verse
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר יעקב holds that the Torah wrote the law for the ערל and also for the טמא, and both verses are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is written about this case (the ערל), and it is written about that case (the טמא), and both are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for רב אחא בר יעקב. He says we cannot learn the טמא from the ערל, so the Torah had to teach each one on its own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the classic 'צריכי' answer: each case has its own unique features, so one cannot be learned from the other. If the Torah had taught only one case, we might think the other is different. So the verse 'בערב תאכלו מצות' really is needed for the טמא, and it cannot prove that מצה is an independent Torah obligation today.

keyTerms.meaning: It is written about this one
And both are necessary (one cannot be learned from the other)

steps.confusionAlert: 'צריכי' does not mean the two verses repeat each other for no reason. It means each verse teaches something that could not have been learned from the other.

phrases.english: It is written regarding this one
and it is written regarding that one, and they are both necessary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 18 and defends רב אחא בר יעקב.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ערל and the טמא cannot be learned from each other, so each one needs its own verse. The verse 'בערב תאכלו מצות' is used for the טמא.
steps.whyThisMatters: Both positions now stand. Each side has an answer for how it reads the verse, so the גמרא turns to a ברייתא to support רבא.

steps.title: A ברייתא supporting רבא begins: eating מצה all week is optional
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא that supports רבא learns from 'ששת ימים תאכל מצות' that eating מצה on the seventh day is optional, and so it is also optional on the first six days.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא was taught that agrees with רבא: 'Six days you shall eat מצות, and on the seventh day there shall be a solemn gathering to ה׳ your God.' Just as the seventh day is optional, so too the six days are optional.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins bringing a ברייתא that supports רבא. The first part teaches that eating מצה on the days of פסח is optional, not required.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Elsewhere the Torah says to eat מצה for seven days, but here it says only 'six days.' This shows that on the seventh day eating מצה is רשות. The ברייתא then applies the same rule to the first six days. The support for רבא comes from the continuation, which will show that the first night is a fixed Torah obligation.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא was taught that agrees with him
A solemn gathering / day of holding back from work
Optional, not required
Just as ... so too

steps.confusionAlert: 'רשות' does not mean you may eat חמץ. It only means there is no positive מצוה to eat מצה on those days. The ban on חמץ stays in full force all week.

phrases.english: It was taught in accordance with Rava:
'Six days you shall eat matzot,
and on the seventh day shall be a solemn assembly to the Lord your God.'
Just as the seventh day is optional,
phrases.notes: Eating מצה on the seventh day is not required.

phrases.english: so too the six days are optional.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After both sides have defended their readings, the גמרא brings outside support for רבא.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's view that eating מצה on the first night is a Torah obligation even today.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא on 'ששת ימים תאכל מצות' (דברים טז:ח). Its later part fixes the first night as a חיוב.

steps.title: Why does the seventh day teach about all the days?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the optional status of the seventh day should apply to the first six days as well.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: This is a short setup question. The גמרא asks how the ברייתא could take a rule about the seventh day and apply it to the other six.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse only singles out the seventh day. It is not obvious why that should change the law for the other days. The גמרא wants the rule of דרשה behind this.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the logic behind the ברייתא's 'מה ... אף' comparison in Step 20.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The rule of דרשה that lets the seventh day's law apply to all seven days.

steps.title: The rule: something taken out of a general rule teaches about the whole rule
steps.stepSummary: The seventh day was included in 'seven days you shall eat מצות' and was singled out. Under the rule of 'דבר שהיה בכלל ויצא', it teaches about all the days.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is something that was included in a general rule and was taken out of the general rule to teach. It was not taken out to teach only about itself. It was taken out to teach about the entire general rule.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with one of the thirteen rules for learning the Torah. Because the seventh day was pulled out of the larger group, its law of 'optional' spreads to the whole group.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One verse says 'שבעת ימים מצות תאכלו', which includes the seventh day. Another verse, 'ששת ימים תאכל מצות', pulls the seventh day out and makes it רשות. By the rule of 'דבר שהיה בכלל ויצא מן הכלל ללמד', what is said about the item pulled out applies to the whole group. So all seven days are רשות.

keyTerms.meaning: Something that was included in a general rule
And was taken out of the general rule to teach
About the entire general rule

steps.whatToRemember: According to this ברייתא, eating מצה on all seven days of פסח is רשות, learned through 'דבר שהיה בכלל ויצא מן הכלל ללמד'. The next part of the ברייתא will show that the first night is different and is a fixed חיוב, which supports רבא.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is why halacha holds that only the first night (and the second night in חוץ לארץ) has a required מצוה of eating מצה. The rest of פסח is only a ban on חמץ.

phrases.english: It is something that was included in the general rule,
phrases.notes: The seventh day was included in 'seven days you shall eat מצות' (שמות יב:טו).

phrases.english: and was taken out of the general rule to teach,
phrases.notes: It gets taken out by the verse 'six days you shall eat מצות'.

phrases.english: it was not taken out to teach about itself alone,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא לְלַמֵּד עַל הַכְּלָל כּוּלּוֹ יָצָא.
phrases.english: but rather it was taken out to teach about the entire general rule.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָוֵי דָּבָר שֶׁהָיָה בַּכְּלָל וְיָצָא מִן הַכְּלָל לְלַמֵּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 21 by naming the rule of דרשה behind the ברייתא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: By the rule of 'דבר שהיה בכלל ויצא מן הכלל ללמד', the seventh day's optional status applies to all the days of פסח.

steps.title: Maybe the first night is also optional
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא suggests that, since eating מצה is optional on all seven days, maybe it is optional on the first night too.
steps.simpleTranslation: I might have thought that even the first night is optional.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא raises a possible mistake. It sets up the next line, which will show that the first night is different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 22 said the optional status of the seventh day teaches about all the days. Someone could stretch that rule to cover the first night as well. The ברייתא raises this idea only so that it can reject it.

keyTerms.meaning: 'I might have thought', a suggestion the ברייתא is about to reject
The first night of פסח (the סדר night)
Optional, not required

phrases.english: I might have thought that even the first night is optional,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It tests how far the 'all days are optional' rule from step 22 reaches.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is eating מצה on the first night also only optional?

steps.title: The first night is required, from the verse about the קרבן פסח
steps.stepSummary: The verse 'על מצות ומרורים יאכלוהו' shows that eating מצה on the first night is an obligation.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says: 'With מצות and bitter herbs they shall eat it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers that the first night is not optional. The Torah commands eating the קרבן פסח together with מצה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The קרבן פסח is eaten on the first night, and the Torah says it must be eaten 'with מצות'. So eating מצה that night is a command, not a choice. This sets apart the first night from the other days.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The verse teaches', introducing the verse that proves the point
Bitter herbs (מרור)
'They shall eat it', meaning the קרבן פסח

steps.confusionAlert: This verse ties the מצה to eating the קרבן פסח. That is exactly why the next step asks what happens when there is no קרבן פסח.

phrases.english: the verse states: 'With matzot and bitter herbs they shall eat it.'
phrases.notes: במדבר ט:יא, said about the קרבן פסח

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: עַל מַצּוֹת וּמְרוֹרִים יֹאכְלוּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It rejects the suggestion of step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The first night is an obligation, because the Torah commands eating the פסח with מצות.

steps.title: What about when there is no בית המקדש
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks how we know there is a first-night obligation of מצה when the בית המקדש is not standing.
steps.simpleTranslation: I only know this when the בית המקדש is standing. When the בית המקדש is not standing, how do I know?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא points out a gap in the last proof. It sets up the next line, which will fill that gap.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse in step 24 links מצה to the קרבן פסח. Without a בית המקדש there is no קרבן פסח, so maybe there is also no obligation of מצה. This is the same question that רבא dealt with earlier.

keyTerms.meaning: 'I only know', meaning the proof so far covers only this case
When the בית המקדש is standing
'From where do we know?', asking for a source

phrases.aramaic: אֵין לִי אֶלָּא בִּזְמַן שֶׁבֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ קַיָּים,
phrases.english: I have only the case when the Temple is standing;

phrases.aramaic: בִּזְמַן שֶׁאֵין בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ קַיָּים מִנַּיִן?
phrases.english: when the Temple is not standing, from where do we know?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵין לִי אֶלָּא בִּזְמַן שֶׁבֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ קַיָּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It notes that the proof in step 24 depends on the קרבן פסח.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source for the מצה obligation when there is no בית המקדש and no קרבן פסח.

steps.title: The Torah made מצה an obligation on its own
steps.stepSummary: The verse 'בערב תאכלו מצות' makes eating מצה on the first night a separate obligation, even without the קרבן פסח. This supports רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says: 'In the evening you shall eat מצות.' The Torah set it as an obligation.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a second verse that commands eating מצה on its own, not tied to the קרבן פסח. This finishes the proof for רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'בערב תאכלו מצות' does not mention the קרבן פסח at all. So the obligation to eat מצה on the first night stands on its own. It still applies today without a בית המקדש, just as רבא said.

keyTerms.meaning: 'In the evening you shall eat מצות' (שמות יב:יח)
Set it as a required obligation
The verse in the Torah

steps.whatToRemember: Eating מצה on the first night of פסח is a Torah obligation even today. It comes from 'בערב תאכלו מצות'. Eating מצה on the other days is optional.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for why we eat מצה at the סדר as a מצוה from the Torah, even without the קרבן פסח.

phrases.english: the verse states: 'In the evening you shall eat matzot,'
the verse established it as an obligation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It answers the question of step 25 and completes the ברייתא that supports רבא.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: מצה on the first night is a separate Torah obligation, even when there is no בית המקדש, as רבא said.

steps.title: The new משנה about falling asleep during the meal
steps.stepSummary: If some of the group fall asleep, they may still eat the קרבן פסח. If the whole group falls asleep, they may not eat any more.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If some of them fell asleep, they may eat. If all of them fell asleep, they may not eat.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It rules on people who fall asleep in the middle of eating the קרבן פסח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If only some fall asleep, the group meal is still going on, so those who wake up can keep eating. If everyone falls asleep, the meal has fully stopped. Starting again would count as a new meal, which is like eating the פסח in two places, and that is not allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה
They fell asleep
Some of them
All of them

phrases.english: MISHNA:
If some of them fell asleep, they may eat.
If all of them fell asleep, they may not eat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic begins. The משנה moves from the מצה discussion to a break in the קרבן פסח meal.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If some of the group fall asleep, they may keep eating. If all fall asleep, they may not eat any more.
